whatWorks: The palette is exactly the brief's: rust, copper and umber over a near-black ground, with values close enough that nothing spikes out as a highlight. It holds warm across all twelve seeds while still rotating (5527/5658 skew copper, 5396/6051 skew umber), which is the declared variation axis working.

Where members do overlap -- 5527 and 5658 most clearly -- the stacked translucent fills build value into something that reads as MASS rather than as pattern. That accumulation is the correct mechanism for this brief and must not be replaced; it only needs to happen everywhere instead of in two tiles.

The rotation spread (axis-aligned squares mixed with 45-degree diamonds and intermediate angles) breaks any grid read and delivers the irregular, varied interval the direction asks for. Nothing in the sheets reads as a lattice.

findings.whatFails: Nothing on any sheet approaches near-saturation. The densest tiles (5527, 5658) cover maybe a third of the frame; the bottom row is a sparse scatter -- 6182 at 256px is roughly eight small squares on an otherwise black field, and 6313 and 6444 are barely denser. At 120px, 6051/6182/6313/6444 read as near-empty dark tiles with a few motes. The direction's forbidden case is literally present: 5134 has a lone square marooned in the top-left corner and 6182 is nothing but isolated objects.
findings.why: The brief's first and load-bearing claim is 'dense to the point of near-saturation... no rest anywhere... no empty quarter', and thumbnailIntent requires the overall mass and its dense grain to survive at 120px. Half the collection currently has no mass to survive. The variationStrategy does say tokens differ first in density, but the floor of that range still has to be inside the brief -- variation is not licence to ship seeds that are the opposite of the mandate.
findings.specificChange: Increase member count per field by roughly 6-10x and decrease the maximum member size to about 8 percent of canvas width, so that mass comes from many small overlapping members rather than from a few large ones. Then raise the per-seed density FLOOR so the sparsest seed in the collection still fills the frame -- let seeds vary between 'dense' and 'near-saturated', not between 'empty' and 'moderate'.
findings.keep: Keep the overlap-driven value build that already works in 5527 and 5658 -- the translucent stacking is what makes accumulated squares read as mass. Scaling the count up must not be paid for by flattening members to opaque, or the field turns into pattern. Keep the existing size ratio between the largest and smallest members.

findings.whatFails: Every tile is a centred blob with a clean empty black margin on all four sides -- nothing reaches or crosses an edge except a couple of accidents. There is also a systematic vertical bias: the incident piles into the upper-centre and the bottom third is markedly emptier (5265, 5396, 6182, 6313 all have a dead bottom band). The 512 single makes it plainest: a ring of squares at the top, a scattering below, and a hole through the middle occupied only by faint specks.
findings.why: The direction states 'the fields spread wide and reach toward the edges, filling the frame so there is no rest and no isolated object anywhere', and negativeSpace is meant to be only the incidental gap between members, never a margin. What is on screen is precisely a margin -- and a centred vignette silhouette, repeated twelve times, is also the single strongest cue that all twelve tiles are one operation.
findings.specificChange: Widen the positional distribution so members are placed beyond the viewBox on all four sides and are clipped by it, making the field read as continuing past the frame. Remove the vertical centroid bias so no quadrant is systematically emptier than another, and add fill into the centre so the 512's central hole closes.
findings.keep: Keep the irregular, non-uniform placement -- the field must not become an even wash. Clusters and locally denser knots are correct and on brief for 'profusion rather than arrangement'; what has to go is the outer margin and the bottom-third void, not the internal variation of interval.

findings.whatFails: The promised three-layer hierarchy is not in the picture. There are two legible scales -- large squares and a spray of tiny specks -- and the specks sit in their own zone rather than threading through anything: in the 512 they occupy the hole beneath the square ring, and in 5265 and 5789 they form a separate cluster below the main mass. At 256px that spray reads as dust or sensor noise on a mostly empty ground, not as a field. The mid-scale that would tie the two together is missing.
findings.why: focalHierarchy asks for 'a dense primary field with two secondary fields threading through it at different scales', and density asks for 'structure at every scale'. Spatially segregated layers are not threaded layers -- they read as two separate pictures stacked, and the jump from big square to speck with nothing between is why there is nothing to reward a long look.
findings.specificChange: Add a genuine mid-scale field between the large members and the specks -- roughly geometric-mean size, at several times the large field's count. Then give all three fields the SAME spatial support as the primary so they interpenetrate, and increase the small field's member count so its grain reads as texture rather than as scattered dirt.
findings.keep: Keep the smallest scale in the work -- the fine grain is what will make the mass survive at 120px once there is enough of it, and thumbnailIntent explicitly wants grain without individual members resolving. Keep the current largest members as the anchor scale; this is an addition between the layers, not a re-sizing of them.

findings.whatFails: The market rows change the layout rather than the density, and not always in the stated direction. 5003 stress is WIDER and busier than 5003 neutral -- the top band disperses across the whole tile -- and 5003 recovery is more open and more hollow than its own neutral. 5134 stress does thin, but by deleting the lower-left group wholesale rather than thinning the field. 5396 is nearly identical across all three rows, down to the same bright orange square in the same position. Across the rows, members move to different places, so a viewer cannot tell it is the same token.
findings.why: marketTransformation requires stress to thin dramatically and open, recovery to close again, and the difference to be obvious at browse size. One seed inverts it, one seed is inert, and where it works it works by relocation -- which also violates identityAnchors, since the multi-scale overlapping construction is supposed to hold across every state while the member layout is what identifies the token.
findings.specificChange: Pin member positions and rotations to the seed alone so they do not move between states, and derive state from a single count-and-scale multiplier applied to that fixed layout: remove members and decrease their size under stress, restore them in recovery. Require stress to decrease total covered area by at least half relative to neutral on EVERY seed, so no seed can come back inert like 5396 or inverted like 5003.
findings.keep: Keep the palette shift that already accompanies stress -- 5134 stress going more outlined and hotter-edged is a legible, on-brief secondary cue. Keep neutral and recovery close to each other; recovery closing back to the dense state is correct and should not be turned into a third distinct composition.

findings.whatFails: A large share of members are hollow squares -- a thin ring with the ground showing through. At 120px those strokes thin toward invisibility, which is why 6444 and 6051 nearly disappear at browse size while looking populated at 256px, and why 5920's lower half evaporates. The hollow centres also work against the mass read: a ring lets the near-black ground back through the interior of every member, so overlapping members punch holes in each other instead of accumulating.
findings.why: The medium is declared as 'several dense fields of FILLED primitives', paletteIntent wants values close so density reads as mass, and thumbnailIntent requires the mass and its grain to survive at 120px. Outline members deliver the opposite of all three: they lower coverage, reintroduce ground inside the silhouette, and are the first thing lost when the render is downsampled.
findings.specificChange: Replace the outline-only members with filled members carrying differing alpha, so value separation comes from opacity stacking rather than from stroke-versus-ground. If a hollow member is retained as a minority accent, increase its stroke weight to at least ~2 percent of that member's own width so it survives the 120px downsample as a solid ring.
findings.keep: Keep the value range that currently separates near-black members from copper ones -- that close-valued layering is what gives the dense tiles their depth. The fix must not compress everything to one opacity, and it must not brighten the field: the near-black ground and the dark end of the palette have to stay.

overall: The palette and the overlap mechanic are right, and where the seeds are densest the work genuinely looks like the thing the brief describes -- but that is two tiles out of twelve, and the collection as a whole is not a thicket. It is a centred scatter of large squares with a clean black margin on every side, a hole through the middle of the 512, a dead bottom third in most tiles, and a bottom row of seeds that at 120px are effectively empty. The three-layer hierarchy is really two, with the fine specks parked in their own zone instead of threading through, and the hollow-square members subtract coverage exactly where coverage is the whole point. The market rows are the other structural problem: they relocate members rather than thinning a fixed field, so 5003 reads busier under stress, 5396 does not move at all, and no row reads as the same token in a different condition. The route forward is not a redesign -- it is more members, smaller, spread past the edges, filled rather than outlined, with a mid-scale layer added and state expressed as one density multiplier over a seed-pinned layout.
